overview: Ryman Healthcare, founded in Christchurch in 1984, is New Zealand's largest retirement living and aged care provider and the leading integrated operator in Victoria, Australia. It owns and operates 47 large-scale, integrated 'continuum of care' villages (38 in NZ, 9 in Australia) combining independent living, serviced apartments and aged care for over 15,500 residents, and is dual-listed on the NZX (primary) and ASX (foreign exempt, since October 2025). The business is now two years into a balance-sheet and operating reset under CEO Naomi James (appointed November 2024) after a decade of debt-funded, development-led growth left it over-levered heading into a weak NZ/Victoria housing market.

business_model.summary: Ryman sells Occupation Right Agreements (ORAs) that give residents the right to occupy a unit in exchange for an upfront capital sum (the occupation advance) plus ongoing weekly fees; in Australia aged-care residents instead pay Refundable Accommodation Deposits (RADs). ORA/RAD capital is recorded as a resident loan liability on the balance sheet (not revenue) and is refundable when the resident leaves, net of an accrued deferred management fee (DMF, now standardised at ~30% of the ORA price, phased in over the resident's expected tenure -- 9 years for independent units, 4.5 years for serviced apartments following an FY25 accounting change). Cash is generated three ways: (1) new sales of ORAs on newly built units, which fund development capex; (2) resales of existing units when a resident departs, which release the DMF plus any capital gain/loss on the unit versus the original occupation advance back to Ryman; and (3) recurring weekly village fees and government/private aged-care funding that cover day-to-day operating costs. Statutory NPAT is heavily influenced by non-cash IAS-40 fair-value (revaluation) gains/losses on the investment-property portfolio, which is why management reports non-GAAP 'Underlying Profit' (largely discontinued from FY25) and now 'Operating EBITDAF' and 'Free Cash Flow' as the preferred performance measures.
business_model.customer_type: B2C -- individual residents (predominantly 80+) and their families; aged-care revenue also has a large B2G component via NZ Ministry of Health/Support at Home and Australian Commonwealth aged-care subsidies
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~85% of units/residents (38 villages, 8,379 RV units, 3,927 care beds), Australia (Victoria) ~15% (9 villages, 1,580 RV units, 759 care beds); FY26 total revenue NZ$855.6m, up 13% YoY

competitive_position.market_position: Largest retirement village/aged-care operator in New Zealand by units and beds, and the leading integrated operator in Victoria, Australia; historically commanded a valuation premium to peers reflecting scale and brand, though that premium has eroded sharply since FY23 as the balance sheet and earnings reset unfolded

moat_factors.description: Pioneered in NZ; villages combine independent living, serviced apartments and aged care in one community, enabling a 'one move' proposition that lengthens average resident tenure (9 years for independent units) and supports higher-acuity care as residents age, differentiating Ryman from pure-play retirement-village or pure-play aged-care operators

Villages typically house 300-400 residents, generating operating leverage in staffing, procurement and service delivery difficult for smaller operators to replicate; 11-time winner of Reader's Digest Most Trusted Brand (NZ) and repeat 'Best Group Provider' awards
Owns undeveloped land at existing and greenfield sites (independently valued at NZ$376m at Sep-2025) providing embedded, optionality-based future growth once returns clear hurdle rates

Large integrated village developments require scarce, well-located land and lengthy resource-consent/planning processes, which is a natural barrier, but is a much weaker moat than switching costs or network effects

weaknesses: Highly capital-intensive, debt-funded growth model that proved fragile when property markets slowed and interest rates rose
Cash generation (resale margins, settlement timing) is directly linked to the health of the residential housing market in NZ and Victoria, a factor outside management's control
Two equity raises in three years (NZ$902m in FY23, ~NZ$1.0bn in Feb-2025) plus a suspended dividend have destroyed significant shareholder value and credibility
Care segment has historically been structurally loss-making/marginal, reliant on government funding settings that are under review in both NZ and Australia

Complex, frequently-revised non-GAAP metrics (Underlying Profit discontinued, Operating EBITDAF and Free Cash Flow introduced, DMF accrual periods changed, cost allocation restated) make like-for-like comparisons difficult and have drawn scrutiny

growth_drivers: Structural demographic tailwind: the 80+ population in NZ/Australia is expected to double by 2050, driving demand for assisted living and higher-acuity care
More than 2,000 units/beds of uncommitted development identified in the FY26 portfolio review in regions with enduring demand, to be pursued only when supported by strong demand and returns
Resident Fund product (rolled out across all NZ villages in FY26) lets care residents draw on retirement-village unit equity to fund care, improving flexibility and capital efficiency
Serviced apartment refinement -- a 'significant near-term opportunity' to improve occupancy and sell-down rates in an under-monetised part of the portfolio

Repricing of the existing book: standard 30% DMF on new contracts (up from ~20.7% in 1H25 to 28.8% in 1H26) and ~60% uplift on weekly fees for rollovers will build into revenue over several years as the ~12%/year portfolio turnover works through

Land bank monetisation: at least NZ$500m targeted cash release by FY29, including an increased ~NZ$250m target from surplus land divestments (seven land bank sites identified as no longer appropriate for development)
Cost-out programme: NZ$57m of annualised savings achieved over two years, with a further NZ$150m targeted sustainable cash-flow improvement by FY29

business.description: Resale volumes, resale margins and settlement timing depend on residential property turnover and price growth; flat house price inflation has compressed gross resale margins from historical highs (e.g. independent-unit resale margin down from ~37% in 1H24 to ~33% in 1H26) and Auckland sales contracting has yet to show meaningful improvement

Aged care and retirement-living segments were disclosed for the first time in 1H26 and are described by management as 'operating significantly below their full potential'; EBITDAF per bed of ~NZ$15-20k/year implies thin margins that depend on occupancy, funding uplifts and cost control

Ryman has invested more than A$2bn in Victoria since 2014; development has been almost completely paused and land sold down, raising the question of whether the AU business is earning its cost of capital and whether the retrenchment represents a permanent scaling-back of the growth thesis

Underlying Profit was discontinued and replaced by Operating EBITDAF/Free Cash Flow; DMF accrual periods, cost allocations and capex classifications have all been revised over FY25-FY26, and a prior-period NZ IAS-40 valuation issue (suspended contributions) required an NZ$77m NTA restatement -- repeated methodology changes complicate trend analysis and have dented investor trust

financial.risk: Legacy leverage and repeated capital raises
financial.description: Gearing peaked near 45% in Sep-2022 before a NZ$902.4m raise (Mar-2023, used to repay USPP notes) cut it to ~33%, followed by a second ~NZ$1.0bn raise in Feb-2025 taking gearing to ~28%; total interest-bearing debt was still NZ$1.58bn at Mar-2026 with total resident-loan liabilities (ORAs/RADs) of ~NZ$6.16bn

A new Interest Cover Ratio covenant of 1.50x commences Sept-2026 (existing waivers applied through Mar-2026); the adjusted total-liabilities-to-net-tangible-assets covenant is capped at 1.0x -- a renewed downturn in valuations or cash flow could pressure headroom despite the FY26 refinancing

Dividends were suspended from FY23 and are not targeted to resume until FY28 (at a payout ratio of 20-50% of cash flow from existing operations per share), meaning income-focused holders have gone roughly five years without a distribution

regulatory.description: A Ministerial Advisory Group is reviewing NZ aged-care funding sustainability, cost-sharing and integration with the health system, with recommendations expected around mid-2026 and government changes targeted for 2027; retirement-village legislation is also under review, though Ryman states its contract terms are already broadly aligned with proposed changes

The new Australian Aged Care Act took effect 1 November 2025 with a co-contribution funding model, RAD retention of up to 10% over five years (a ~A$6.4m annualised benefit to Ryman), twice-yearly DAP indexation and new care-minute requirements; management expects the changes to be broadly neutral but execution risk remains

macro.description: As a heavily-indebted, capital-intensive developer/operator, Ryman's interest costs, development returns and covenant headroom are directly sensitive to NZ/AU benchmark rates; falling rates over FY25-26 have already meaningfully reduced interest costs (down NZ$28.9m HoH in 1H26) and are a key swing factor for future free cash flow

Post-COVID construction cost escalation was a major driver of the original balance-sheet stress; while now more disciplined and phased, any renewed materials/labour cost inflation would compress development margins on the remaining pipeline

Resale settlement volumes and pricing are tied to the broader residential property cycle in NZ and Victoria; a renewed housing downturn would directly reduce cash release from resales and elongate the path back to sustained free cash flow and dividends

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Structurally favourable long-term demand (80+ population in NZ/Australia expected to double by 2050) set against a sector-wide overhang of elevated retirement-village stock, competitive discounting and slow property-market recovery in the near term; NZ and Australian governments are both actively reviewing aged-care funding models, creating medium-term policy uncertainty but also potential for improved sector economics
macro_factors.cyclicality: High relative to typical healthcare real estate -- new-sale volumes and resale margins are geared to the residential housing cycle and consumer confidence, even though the underlying demand driver (ageing population) is non-cyclical
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High -- large net debt load, development funding needs, and an imputed-interest income/expense mechanism on RADs and resident loans mean net interest costs move materially with NZ/AU benchmark rates
key_input_costs: Construction materials and labour (build cost inflation)
Interest rates on floating and refinanced bank debt
NZD/AUD exchange rate (translation of the Australian investment-property portfolio and RAD balances)

recent_developments.event: Completed dual listing (foreign exempt) on the ASX under ticker RYM, broadening the investor base and funding access; NZX remains the primary listing

Completed full refinancing of ~NZ$2 billion of syndicated bank facilities, extending weighted average tenor to ~4.8-5 years with no bank maturities until FY31 and improved pricing/covenants; new ICR covenant of 1.50x from September 2026

1H26 (six months to 30 Sept 2025) results: first positive free cash flow in a decade (NZ$56.2m, up NZ$108.7m YoY), Operating EBITDAF up 193% to NZ$40.1m, revenue up 13% to NZ$413.8m, but statutory NPAT loss of NZ$45.2m (vs +NZ$82.0m prior year) as fair-value gains collapsed; annualised cost-out target lifted to NZ$50-60m

Investor Day (3 Feb 2026): unveiled refreshed strategy and new capital management framework, including a shift away from rapid development-led growth, a target to release at least NZ$500m in cash by FY29 (incl. ~NZ$250m from land divestments), NZ$150m sustainable cash-flow improvement target by FY29, and guidance for a return to sustainable dividends in FY28 at a 20-50% payout of cash flow from existing operations

FY26 (year to 31 March 2026) full-year results: revenue NZ$855.6m (+13%), Operating EBITDAF NZ$88.3m (+94%), first full-year positive free cash flow in over a decade of NZ$188.3m, statutory net loss narrowed to NZ$171.3m (loss per share NZ$0.17, improved from NZ$0.61 loss in FY25); portfolio review identified seven land bank sites for divestment and more than 2,000 units/beds of uncommitted future development; two ageing Christchurch care centres closed

AGM commentary reiterated turnaround momentum, FY29 cash targets and the FY28 dividend pathway; management flagged 'disappointing' share price performance despite operational progress and reaffirmed confidence in long-term demographic positioning

guidance.as_of: FY26 Annual Report / 1H26 Results (as at May 2026 and Feb 2026 Investor Day)

items.notes: Lifted from prior guidance of 1,100-1,300 following stronger 1H26 sales momentum; FY26 actual came in at 1,410
Lifted from prior guidance of NZ$46 million; NZ$57 million of annualised savings actually achieved over FY25-FY26 combined

items.vs_prior: new (medium-term target set at Feb-2026 Investor Day)
items.notes: Driven by pricing resets, cost efficiencies and rising occupancy; NZ$47 million already delivered in FY26
Includes an increased target of ~NZ$250 million from surplus land divestments; NZ$150 million net cash flow released from developments plus NZ$72 million of land divestment proceeds settled in FY26
Payout policy of 20-50% of cash flow from existing operations (CFEO) per share, conditional on continued execution of the cash and earnings targets

items.target: Reduced from seven to two village sites under construction
items.notes: Reflects the strategic shift away from rapid, development-led growth toward disciplined, phased, return-driven development

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Dean Hamilton and CEO Naomi James described FY26 as marking the reset 'translating into improved performance, cash flow generation, and a stronger balance sheet,' with operating profitability almost doubling and the first full-year positive free cash flow in a decade. Management acknowledged the share price performance 'remains disappointing' despite operational progress, and reiterated confidence in the long-term 80+ demographic tailwind. FY27 priorities are stated as: driving occupancy in recently opened villages, improving sales effectiveness and the serviced apartment offering, and further reducing the operating cost base to offset inflationary pressures.

bull_case: The two-year balance sheet reset appears largely complete: gearing down from ~45% (Sep-2022) to ~28% (Mar-2026), debt refinanced out to a 4.8-5 year average tenor with no bank maturities until FY31 and >NZ$600m of headroom, materially de-risking the equity

First positive full-year free cash flow in over a decade (NZ$188.3m in FY26) and Operating EBITDAF nearly doubling YoY suggest the operating turnaround is gaining real traction, not just accounting adjustment

Repricing of the resident book (standard 30% DMF, ~60% weekly-fee uplift on rollovers) has structurally raised the revenue yield on new contracts; as the ~12%/year portfolio turns over, this should mechanically lift recurring earnings for several years even without volume growth

Powerful, uncontroversial demographic tailwind -- the 80+ population in NZ/Australia is expected to double by 2050 -- underpins long-run demand for Ryman's integrated continuum-of-care model, in which it remains the largest and most awarded operator in NZ

Explicit, quantified medium-term targets (NZ$500m cash release and NZ$150m cash-flow improvement by FY29, dividends resuming FY28) give the market concrete milestones against which to hold management accountable, and land-bank/asset-sale proceeds provide a visible, largely de-risked source of near-term cash
bear_case: Two large equity raises in three years (NZ$902m FY23, ~NZ$1.0bn Feb-2025) plus a five-plus-year dividend suspension have severely diluted and impaired returns for long-term holders, and the stock's persistent underperformance despite the operational 'reset' narrative suggests the market remains skeptical of execution

Cash generation is still fundamentally hostage to the NZ/Victoria residential property cycle: gross resale margins have compressed from ~37% to ~33% (independent units) as house-price inflation has flattened, and Auckland sales contracting has yet to recover meaningfully

Repeated changes to non-GAAP definitions, accounting policies (DMF accrual periods, cost capitalisation, a prior-period NZ$77m NTA restatement) and segment reporting make it hard for investors to have confidence in reported trends, and statutory NPAT remains a large loss (NZ$171.3m in FY26) driven by muted fair-value gains

The near-complete pause of Australian development after >A$2bn invested since 2014 raises the question of whether the AU expansion will ever earn an adequate return on the capital already committed, and the aged-care and retirement-living segments are described by management themselves as operating 'significantly below their full potential'

Regulatory uncertainty is elevated on both sides of the Tasman -- NZ aged-care/retirement-village funding reform recommendations are due around mid-2026 with implementation targeted for 2027, and the new Australian Aged Care Act (Nov-2025) introduces new cost/co-contribution structures -- creating a real, if currently judged 'broadly neutral,' risk to the economics of the core care business
